title: Not carried off in secret
hookLine: Hanuman offers to carry Sita home tonight, and she says no, for reasons worth hearing
carry: maryada: the right way matters, not just the rescue
last: HE DIDN'T KNOW WHERE YOU WERE.

cards: It seems like the obvious ending. The rescuer is here; the captive is right in front of him. Hanuman says it out loud: climb on my back, my lady.
I'll carry you across the sea today, and you'll see Rama. In a different kind of story, that would be the last page.
Sita looks at the small monkey in front of her, and her first reaction is a doubt so practical it's almost funny.

teach.b: You're so small, she says. How could you carry me across the ocean? So Hanuman shows her.
He grows, right there in the grove, until he stands like a mountain, blazing. Sita believes him now. And still she says no.
Valmiki gives her reasons, and each one is real. First, the journey: high over the sea at that speed, she's afraid she'd lose her grip and fall.
Second, the rakshasas would chase them, and Hanuman would have to fight while carrying her.
Third, she will not willingly touch any man but Rama. Ravana seized her by force; that she couldn't help. She won't choose it now.
And fourth, the one she lingers on: let Rama come, defeat Ravana and take me home himself. To be carried off in secret would be unworthy of him. Readers weigh these reasons differently.
But notice: her doubt about Hanuman's size was settled in a moment. The refusal was a decision.

Hindus have a word for what she is guarding: maryada, the right limits, the proper way of doing things. Rama is loved as Maryada Purushottam, the best of men, who keeps them. Sita keeps them too, even as a captive.
Ravana stole her in secret; she won't be stolen back the same way. In this story, how a thing is done is part of whether it is dharma.

how: Sita's refusal to be carried away by Hanuman is a discussed passage; many Hindu tellings read it as dignity and maryada, and Rama is widely praised as Maryada Purushottam.

games.q: you're Sita. a mountain-sized Hanuman can fly you home tonight, in secret. by maryada, what do you say?
o: yes, at once: getting out is all that counts.
no: Rama should come and win me back openly.
games.why: Sita declines: she might fall, the rakshasas would pursue, she won't willingly touch another man, and a secret rescue would be unworthy of Rama. the way matters.

practice: Call up a shortcut someone has offered you, or one you've been tempted by. If you pray, hold it before Rama, Maryada Purushottam, and ask quietly: is this the right way, or just a way?
If you don't pray, name its risks, one with each breath, the way Sita named hers. Then ask what the slower, cleaner way would protect. There's no need to decide yet.

wordCard.voice: Her doubt. Sita's doubt that a small monkey could carry her, settled when Hanuman grows, and her refusal, for safety, for her own choice and for Rama's honor.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Hindi maryādā, a boundary or limit: the right way of doing things; Rama is Maryādā Puruṣottama.

carryVoice: Your line: maryada, the right way matters, not just the rescue. Tomorrow, the monkey who crossed an ocean calls himself the smallest. That's the week.
